Instead, when the hydrogen-rich gas reacts with the fluidized coal, it also reacts with the sulfur in the coal. The result is the formation of lethal hydrogen sulfide gas in significant quantities. All H<sub>2</sub>S must be captured, along with other by-products of the reaction such as various aromatic organic compounds, trace elements, and ammonia. The hydrogen sulfide is reduced to elemental sulfur. Other trapped compounds such as ammonia can be burned or, more profitably, sold or used for reclamation purposes. Some waste compounds appear in plant waste water. Very sophisticated treatment is required to purify these waste waters.
In practice, a slight amount of 
H_2S
 would escape through the sulfur plant vent. For example, it is anticipated that the El Paso Natural Gas Company plant proposed for the Four Corners area of New Mexico would release about 6.6 ppm from this vent. With a proper stack design, this can be decreased to well below 0.1 ppm at ground level. The design would have to be specific for the plant site choosen. Even very small concentrations of 
H_2S
 would be detectable by the typical "rotten egg" odor.
Since heat from external sources is required in several of the processes, and because an onsite power generation facility is assumed, not all combustion of the coal occurs within closed vessels. Therefore, there would be the usual need to control fly ash, sulfur dioxide, and oxides of nitrogen, and some of these will be discharged from furnaces, boilers, etc. unless adequate precautions are taken.
